---
title: "How opus's data dictionaries were built"
---

The information needed to read ICES DATRAS data correctly is real but
scattered — spread across a WSDL, a separately maintained metadata service,
a vocabulary server, and a hand-kept spreadsheet, none of which fully
agrees with the others. This page describes how those are reconciled into
two machine-readable specifications, what the R functions around them are
for, and the failure modes the design guards against.

The dictionaries are built once and maintained by hand. The seeding and
curation scripts under `data-raw/` are kept as provenance — *how did this
entry come to say that?* — not as a rebuild path. Re-running them would
overwrite hand-made decisions with whatever the live sources happen to say
today.

## Why a structured dictionary at all

Anyone reading DATRAS answers the same questions repeatedly. What type is
this field? What does code `4` mean here? Is `-9` a missing value or an
answer? Which of these two similarly named columns is the one I want? Each
consumer rediscovers those answers independently, usually by trial and
error against real data, and usually without writing down what they
learned.

Consolidating them buys two things worth insisting on. The result is
**authoritative** — every claim traced to a primary source and checked
against real data. And it is **portable**: the deliverable is YAML
conforming to a published specification, not an R object. The R package is
thin tooling around those files. If nobody runs it again, the dictionaries
remain usable by any language that can read a text file.

## Four sources, reconciled

No single source is sufficient, and none is trustworthy alone.

**The WSDL** is the primary authority for field types. Each operation's
description page embeds a sample response generated from the server's
actual return type, so it cannot drift from what the service sends the way
a hand-maintained table can. This is not a theoretical preference: where
the WSDL and the metadata service disagree, real data has repeatedly proved
the WSDL right.

**`getDatrasFieldList`** documents field names and the legacy names they
were renamed from. It is separately maintained rather than generated from
the live operations, and it is demonstrably unreliable — it covers 22 of
LT's 58 real fields, claims fields that do not exist, omits others
entirely, and pairs at least one field with a legacy name that is not real.
It is used, but never on its own authority.

**icesVocab** supplies code semantics — what the values in a coded field
mean. It carries no structural type information, and its keys are tied to
each field's *legacy* name rather than its current one, a dependency that
stays invisible until it produces a wrong answer.

**The DATRAS field-description spreadsheet** is the closest thing to a
Technical Reference and the only source for some descriptive text. It is
hand-maintained and not kept in step with the other three.

The reconciliation rule that follows: **a claim is trusted when two
independent sources agree, or when one source agrees with real data.**
Never because a single document says so.

## Why not `icesDatras` as the access layer

The obvious shortcut is to let ICES's own R package
([`ices-tools-prod/icesDatras`](https://github.com/ices-tools-prod/icesDatras))
handle retrieval and parsing. opus calls the web services directly instead,
and the reason is specific rather than general.

`icesDatras` is a convenience layer that does not merely fetch — it
*corrects*. `getDATRAS()` takes `fix_types` and `new_names` arguments, both
defaulting from global options, and both applied from a schema table
bundled inside the package. `applyDatrasNameSchema()` renames columns by
mapping `FieldNameOld` to `FieldName` from that table; `fix_types` (on by
default) coerces column types from the same source.

That bundled table derives from `getDatrasFieldList` — the source opus
independently finds to contain errors. So its corrections carry those
errors forward, applied silently. Concretely, the bundled schema renames
CA's `Age` to `IndividualAge`; the live `getCAdata` operation returns
`Age`, and there is no `IndividualAge` anywhere in real CA data. A
consumer who opts into `new_names` receives a column named for a field
that does not exist.

For most users that is a reasonable trade — a maintained package that
smooths over an awkward service is worth having, and ICES ships it as the
supported way in. It is the wrong foundation for *this* project
specifically, because opus's job is to document where ICES's own metadata
is wrong. A layer that quietly applies that metadata's corrections removes
the very signal opus exists to capture: the discrepancy stops being
visible to measure, and the result would be "true, as filtered through
another package's assumptions."

So opus reads the WSDL, `getDatrasFieldList` and icesVocab directly and
verifies each claim against at least two independent live sources. The
distinction matters in one direction only: opus does not need a *better*
client than `icesDatras`, it needs an *unmediated* one.

## The build

Three phases, keyed throughout by ICES's legacy field names, with opus's
own names introduced exactly once at the end.

**Seed.** Crawl the live sources and assemble a first-pass dictionary: one
entry per real field, typed from the WSDL, with whatever ICES documents
attached. The seed records what the sources say, including where they
contradict each other.

**Curate.** Work the seed against the real archive. Every range, every
constraint, every enum membership is checked against actual values before
it is written down. Codes are enriched from icesVocab where a field
resolves to a controlled list. Where sources conflict, the conflict is
resolved against data and the resolution recorded, not silently applied.

**Rename.** Translate legacy names to opus's curated names as a single,
pure, positional rename — no other change in the same step. Keeping it
isolated is what makes it auditable: the two files are one specification
under two naming schemes, and any divergence between them is a bug rather
than a design.

Both files ship. `DATRAS-data-dict-legacy.yaml` is not an archive copy:
submitters send ICES data under legacy names, so it is the submission-side
specification.

## What the functions are for

The package is thin but not arbitrary. Each exported function exists
because some consumer — the curation flow, the archive build, or a
downstream package — needs to ask one question without re-implementing the
answer. The [function reference](reference.qmd) lists them all; what
follows is why the groups exist.

**Reading the service.** `op_datras_operations()` lists what the DATRAS
service exposes; `op_datras_operation_types()` returns the fields and types
one operation actually returns. Everything needing to know what ICES really
sends goes through these rather than parsing the service again.

`op_datras_operations()` doubles as a migration tripwire. ICES is renaming
DATRAS fields one table at a time, and each converted table appears as a
new `…NewHeaders` operation. Watching that list is how the migration's
progress becomes visible without being announced.

**Names.** `op_datras_field_metadata()` returns `getDatrasFieldList` as
ICES publishes it — what ICES claims. `op_datras_field_list()` returns what
survives cross-checking against each operation's real response, tagging
every mapping with the evidence behind it. `op_datras_rename_crosswalk()`
reduces that to a collision-checked 1:1 map for callers that just need to
rename columns.

**The specification.** `op_field_spec()` returns the dictionary as a plain
data frame — legacy name, current name, type. That one accessor is the
whole contract between opus and anything downstream, so no consumer parses
the YAML itself.

**Conversion.** Four functions turn a parsed XML table into publishable
parquet, and the order is load-bearing:

```r
df <- op_cast_wsdl_types(df, "HL")   # physical types; sentinels untouched
df <- op_rename_to_new(df, "HL")     # legacy -> current names
df <- op_strip_sentinels(df, "HL")   # -9 -> NA, where it means absence
df <- op_cast_to_spec(df, "HL")      # semantic types the wire can't express
```

Casting is first because the WSDL type map is keyed by each operation's own
field names, which are the legacy ones. Renaming precedes sentinel
resolution because the sentinel registry is keyed by current names. The
semantic cast is last because a date column cannot hold `-9`.

Because these are exported rather than buried in a build script, a
downstream package can produce results identical to the published archive
by calling the same four functions on its own live fetch, instead of
reimplementing the rules and slowly diverging from them.

**Sentinels.** `op_sentinels()` reads the registry, `op_sentinel_policy()`
resolves it into a per-column verdict with the reasoning attached, and
`op_sentinel_audit()` measures a real parquet file against it. The audit is
both the evidence behind each decision and the regression check afterwards.

**Validation.** `op_validate_spec()` checks the dictionary is well-formed,
`op_validate_meta()` checks a dataset's names and types against it, and
`op_validate_data()` checks the values. These matter more than usual under
hand-maintenance: they are what makes editing a large YAML by hand safe,
and `op_validate_meta()` is the gate saying the published data and the
specification still describe each other.

## What the design guards against

Most of the hazards here share a shape: they produce a plausible result
instead of an error. That is what the following are built to prevent.

### A metadata service that disagrees with its own data

Taking `getDatrasFieldList` at face value produces wrong answers, so
`op_datras_field_list()` **grades** it rather than discarding it. A rename
is accepted when the legacy name actually appears in that operation's live
response; accepted at lower confidence when another table confirms the same
mapping; and otherwise recorded as unverified rather than acted on.

That middle tier carries real weight. Most of LT's renames resolve only
that way — its fields are renamed exactly as their HH counterparts are, but
ICES documents the rename only for HH. Without cross-table evidence the
majority of that table would keep its legacy names.

### Evidence that vanishes when the question narrows

Because that middle tier borrows evidence *between* tables, asking about
one table alone leaves nothing to borrow from — and the honest failure
would be an error, not a smaller answer. Resolution therefore always runs
over the full set of tables and narrows at the end, so no caller can ask
the question in a way that quietly degrades the result.

### Guards that can pass vacuously

A check written as "is this table name among the dictionary's keys" passes
for every input when those keys are `tables` and `glossary` — never a table
name. Such a guard converts a loud failure into a silent one, and a type
caster built on it does nothing at all while appearing to work.

Types therefore come from an explicit per-column cast against the WSDL,
applied to every typed column rather than only the numeric ones, and an
unrecognised type is reported rather than passed through. Otherwise a
column can be integer in files where every value happens to be a sentinel
and text in files with a real value.

### A value that means two things

DATRAS uses `-9` to mean "not recorded". In some fields it is an answer:
for tickler chains it means *none were used*, an icesVocab-documented code
and the dominant value in that column rather than a rare one. Replacing it
wholesale destroys real data, and once destroyed the evidence needed to
notice is gone with it.

The opposite reflex is also wrong. Parquet has a native null, so carrying
`-9` onward makes every downstream consumer rediscover the convention, with
any naive average silently incorrect.

What resolves it is that neither the value nor its frequency is the
discriminator. Two fields can both be almost entirely `-9` — one because
nobody records that measurement, one because "none" is the usual answer.
What separates them is the **label ICES publishes for the code**: a set
meaning absence (`Not known`, `Not available`, `Unknown`, …) against a much
smaller set naming a real answer (`No ticklers are allowed`, `No plus
group`, `Invalid hauls`).

So the policy strips by default, keeps where the vocabulary documents the
sentinel as a real answer, and records the label list in the known-issues
registry where it can be reviewed. Anything the list does not recognise
resolves to *keep*: an unrecognised label must never silently destroy a
documented code.

That `-9` carries both meanings inside one vocabulary is an ICES-side
defect, not a modelling choice, and it is recorded as such.

### Ordering that turns a correct conversion into data loss

`DateofCalculation` arrives as `YYYYMMDD` and should be a date. Converting
it while sentinels are still present turns every `-9` into a null — a
conversion that is individually correct and collectively destructive, and
one that reports nothing.

Sentinel resolution therefore runs first, as a declared decision recorded
in the registry, and only then does the date conversion. As a backstop
`op_cast_to_spec()` **refuses** to convert a column containing anything it
cannot parse rather than producing nulls. A conversion that cannot be done
losslessly is an error, not a result.

### A specification that does not describe its own data

Validating opus's output against opus's specification is the check that
catches drift between the two. It surfaces a consistent class of mismatch:
fields typed `enum` whose data is stored as integers. Under the dictionary
specification an enum's underlying data must be string-like, so those are
genuine violations.

Resolving them needs a judgement rather than a rule, because the options
are not equivalent. A number column may not carry a code-to-label map, so
retyping a field to a number **deletes its labels** from both the
dictionary and the published catalog. For quarter and month that costs
nothing — the labels restate the number. For tickler counts and species
categories, where the codes are not self-explanatory, the labels are the
useful part, and those fields stay enums stored as text.

The general point: "make the validator pass" is not the goal. The validator
identifies where description and data disagree; which of the two should
move is a question about what the specification is for.

## Keeping it rigorous

A few habits do most of the work.

**Real data outranks any document.** Where a source and the archive
disagree, the archive wins and the source becomes an issue to report.

**Two sources, or one plus data.** No structural claim rests on a single
document, including ICES's own.

**Audits are exhaustive, not sampled.** Both name schemes are checked, not
just the current one; every vocabulary prefix candidate, not just the first
that resolves; every column, not a handful.

**Prefer a loud failure.** A check that can pass vacuously is treated as a
defect, and a function that cannot do its job correctly stops rather than
returning something plausible.

## Scope

This describes how the metadata *specification* is built. It is not domain
QC and not data transformation — that work belongs downstream, in
obus/imbus's own workpackages. opus's boundary is what a field is called,
what type it is, what its values may be, and where ICES's own documentation
of that is wrong.

For the code-level detail behind several sections above, see
[Technical notes](technical-notes.qmd). For the findings reported back to
ICES, see [Issues found](issues.qmd).
